details:
**"The Raven"**
Poe's most famous poem (1845). On a "midnight dreary" in "bleak December," a grieving speaker mourning his lost Lenore hears "a tapping, as of some one gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door." A "grim, ungainly, ghastly" ebony bird enters, perches "upon a bust of Pallas" (Athena) above the door, and answers every question with "Nevermore."

**"Is there balm in Gilead?" and "Night's Plutonian shore"**
Lines from "The Raven." The speaker asks the bird, whom he calls a "prophet," whether there is "balm in Gilead" (comfort, an allusion to the Book of Jeremiah) and whether he will meet Lenore in the afterlife. He calls the bird a visitor from "Night's Plutonian shore" and recalls "dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before."

**"The Tell-Tale Heart"**
A short story whose insane narrator insists he is sane while describing how he murdered an old man because of his "pale blue eye," a "vulture eye." He shines a lantern on the sleeping man's eye for several nights, kills him, and hides the body under the floorboards. When police visit, he hears the dead man's heart beating like "a watch enveloped in cotton," and, thinking the officers are mocking his horror, he shrieks, "I admit the deed!"

**"The Cask of Amontillado"**
A revenge story in which Montresor, whose family motto is "Nemo me impune lacessit" ("No one attacks me with impunity"), lures the wine connoisseur Fortunato into his family catacombs during carnival with the promise of tasting a cask of Amontillado. Fortunato, wearing a jester's cap with bells, mocks the rival judge Luchresi and makes a Masonic sign that Montresor answers with a trowel; Montresor then chains him in a niche and walls him up alive.

**"The Masque of the Red Death"**
A story in which Prince Prospero shuts himself and a thousand nobles inside a fortified, castellated abbey to escape a plague called the Red Death. He holds a masquerade ball in seven rooms of different colors, the last black with blood-red windows, where an ebony clock chimes every hour and the dancers stop. A figure in a blood-spattered burial shroud appears, Prospero pursues it, and all die; the story ends with the Red Death holding "illimitable dominion over all."

**"The Fall of the House of Usher"**
A story in which the narrator visits his sickly friend Roderick Usher, whose crumbling mansion has a fissure running down its front and stands above a dark tarn. Roderick sings his poem "The Haunted Palace," and he and the narrator entomb his twin sister Madeline, who still has a faint blush on her cheeks, in a vault. While the narrator reads aloud from "The Mad Trist" by Sir Launcelot Canning, about the knight Ethelred, a dragon, and a brass shield, the sounds in the story are echoed in the house; Madeline, buried alive, emerges and falls dead on Roderick, and the house collapses into the tarn.

**C. Auguste Dupin and "The Murders in the Rue Morgue"**
Poe created the first modern fictional detective, C. Auguste Dupin, who solves crimes by "ratiocination." In "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" (1841), Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter Camille, who is found stuffed up a chimney, are murdered; the bank clerk Adolphe Le Bon is wrongly arrested, witnesses disagree about the nationality of a shrill voice heard along with a "gruff" one, and Dupin deduces that the killer was an orangutan, using hair found in Madame L'Espanaye's hand. The story opens with Dupin reading the narrator's mind about the actor Chantilly and a discussion of how checkers taxes analysis more than chess.

**"The Purloined Letter"**
The third Dupin story, in which Minister D— steals a compromising letter from a royal lady. The Prefect G— searches D—'s hotel exhaustively, even taking the legs off furniture, but Dupin finds it hidden in plain sight in a card rack, arranges a distraction in the street (a man firing a musket) to swap it for a facsimile, and collects a 50,000-franc reward. The story includes the guessing game "even and odd" with marbles and was famously debated by Jacques Lacan and Jacques Derrida; the second Dupin story is "The Mystery of Marie Rogêt."

**"The Conqueror Worm" and "Ligeia"**
"The Conqueror Worm" is a poem about a "gala night" where angels watch a play, "the tragedy, 'Man,'" performed by "mimes, in the form of God on high," while "the orchestra breathes fitfully / The music of the spheres"; a "blood-red thing that writhes" devours the actors, and its hero is the Conqueror Worm. The poem appears in the story "Ligeia," about the narrator's brilliant first wife Ligeia, who seems to return from death in the body of his second wife, Lady Rowena.

**"The Bells"**
A four-part sound poem about sledge bells, wedding bells, alarm bells, and funeral bells. Poe coined the word "tintinnabulation" for their sound, as they keep "time, time, time," and the poem describes the "gush of euphony" that "voluminously wells" from the golden wedding bells.

**"The Gold-Bug"**
A story in which William Legrand, bitten by a gold-colored scarab beetle ("scarabaeus") whose markings resemble a death's head, deciphers a cryptogram and, with his servant Jupiter and the narrator, finds Captain Kidd's buried treasure.

**"The Black Cat"**
A story in which an alcoholic narrator gouges out an eye of his cat Pluto and later hangs it; that night his house burns down. A second cat appears with a patch of white fur that slowly grows into the shape of a gallows; when he tries to kill it, he kills his wife instead and walls her up in the cellar, but the cat's cry from behind the wall reveals the body to the police.

**"Annabel Lee" and other poems**
In "Annabel Lee," Poe's last complete poem, angels "went envying" the lovers and sent a wind that killed the speaker's beloved "in a kingdom by the sea." Other poems used as clues: "Alone" ("From childhood's hour I have not been / As others were"), "A Dream Within a Dream" ("Take this kiss upon the brow!" and "All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream"), "Ulalume," in which Psyche shows the speaker his lost love's tomb, "The City in the Sea," where Death "has reared himself a throne," and "Sonnet—To Science," which calls science "True daughter of Old Time," asks "Why preyest thou thus upon the poet's heart," and accuses it of dragging Diana from her car.

**"The Pit and the Pendulum" and "Hop-Frog"**
In "The Pit and the Pendulum," a prisoner of the Spanish Inquisition in Toledo is tied beneath a descending razor-edged pendulum and then forced toward a pit by the heated iron walls of his cell, until the French army under General Lasalle arrives and rescues him. In "Hop-Frog," a crippled jester tricks the king and seven councilors into wearing tar-covered orangutan costumes and sets them ablaze.

**"Berenice," "Morella," The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym, and other works**
In "Berenice," the narrator, who obsesses over his cousin's teeth and a line from Tertullian beginning "Mortuus est Dei filius," finds thirty-two teeth in a box after her burial. In "Morella," the learned wife (a student of Fichte and Schelling) dies giving birth to a daughter who, when named Morella, also dies, and the mother's body has vanished from the tomb. Poe's only novel, The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym, follows Pym, who stows away on the whaler Grampus with his dog Tiger and later sails toward the South Pole with Dirk Peters. "The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether" depicts an asylum whose patients have overthrown their keepers, and Stéphane Mallarmé's sonnet "The Tomb of Edgar Poe" praises the poet who gave "a purer sense to the words of the tribe."
